title: State transitions for edit distance
summary: When transforming book into code, the last characters k and e differ. Insertion, deletion, and replacement each leave a different pair of prefixes to transform.
context: Let state dp[i, j] be the minimum number of edits needed to transform the first i characters of source string s into the first j characters of target string t, where each insertion, deletion, or replacement costs 1. Using s = book and t = code (current prefix lengths i = 4 and j = 4), this figure examines where the state transitions come from when the current final characters s[i-1] = k and t[j-1] = e differ.
description: On the left is the current state dp[i, j], and on the right from top to bottom are the three branches for insertion (appending), deletion, and replacement. Grayed-out final characters indicate characters already matched or deleted and no longer part of the remaining prefixes to be solved.

After insertion, the newly appended final character matches and cancels the target's final character without consuming any character of the original source string, so only j decreases by 1. Deletion removes only the source's final character, so only i decreases by 1. After replacement, the two final characters match and cancel each other, so both i and j decrease by 1.

Following the three branches in order, the table below distinguishes "Source after edit" from "Remaining source prefix" and lists the corresponding subproblem state; the figure does not compute the final edit distance from book to code.

frames.title: Three edit operations reduce the problem to different remaining prefixes
frames.explanation: Each of the three operations costs 1 edit, and we choose whichever leaves the fewest edits in its remaining subproblem; therefore, when the final characters differ, dp[i,j] = min(dp[i,j-1], dp[i-1,j], dp[i-1,j-1]) + 1.
